paragraphs.text: 1 In the second year of Darius the king, in the sixth month, in the first day of the month, came the word of the LORD by Haggai the prophet unto Zerubbabel the son of Shealtiel, governor of Judah, and to Joshua the son of Josedech, the high priest, saying, 2 "Thus speaketh the LORD of hosts, saying, This people say, The time is not come, the time that the LORD's house should be built."
In the introduction to the prophecy he specified its date, to whom it was delivered, to whom it was addressed, and its subject:

First: as for its date, the prophet uttered it on the first day of the sixth month (Elul) in the second year of Darius the Persian king. Perhaps he met with those celebrating the monthly feast, for the Jews were accustomed (to this day, as regards the Orthodox among them) to gather on the first of the lunar month for communal worship. The prophet took advantage of the gathering to proclaim the explicit and effective word of the Lord.

Second: the prophecy was delivered "by Haggai the prophet" (literally, by the hand of Haggai the prophet)... How is a prophecy delivered into a hand? St. Augustine says: [The word "hand" here means "power," and the word of prophecy was delivered into the hands of the prophets like a strong sword that shatters evil. They received the word of God in their hands with power, to speak what they wished to those with whom they wished to speak, neither fearing power nor despising poverty. In their hands is a (spiritual) sword that they draw whenever they wish, holding it and striking. All this is within the authority of the preachers].

Third: the prophet directed the prophetic word to the governor and the priest, who had been enthusiastic for the work but whom external and internal opposition had stopped. The governor is called "Zerubbabel," a grandson of King Jehoiachin of the seed of David; his name means (born in Babylon). He is also called Sheshbazzar, appointed by Cyrus the Persian as governor over Judah (Ezra 5:14). As for Joshua the son of Josedech the high priest, his name means (Jehovah is salvation) and his father's name means (Jehovah is righteousness); we have spoken before about him as a type of the Great High Priest, Jesus Christ, our salvation and our righteousness in the Father.

In our study of the book of Zechariah we saw the governor as a symbol of the human will, which God established in man to direct life in the Lord like a king with authority over soul, body, mind and feelings, while the priest points to the heart that is sanctified to God by the Holy Spirit, in which our Christ dwells as the Bishop of our souls and our Intercessor by His blood with His Father. If the prophetic speech there was directed to the governor and the priest, it is because the word of God addresses the human will and the heart together. For the temple of the Lord will not be built in us unless our will bows and our heart submits before God, saying: "Behold the handmaid of the Lord; be it unto me according to thy word." In other words, in order to enjoy the divine sanctuary whose foundations were laid in the waters of Baptism by the Holy Spirit, and which is even being formed within us to increase in glory day by day by the work of God in us, it behooves us to hand over our inner Zerubbabel and our Joshua into His hands, that is, to hand over to Him the living will working with the heart with all its feelings.

Truly our will is "Zerubbabel," for it was born in Babylon, where we were under the captivity of sin; but the Lord alone frees it from its captivity and sends it forth to the heavenly Jerusalem, not to lead fifty thousand men to work, but to carry within itself the energies and possibilities of the Lord Himself in it, that He may work through it and through all its gifts and feelings... for the sake of His Kingdom.

Just as we need the sanctification of the will by freeing it from its violent captivity through the work of the Cross, so we need the sanctification of the heart also, so that the true Joshua may dwell in it, that is, our Jesus, who is "God our Savior" and at the same time is our "Josedech," that is, (God our righteousness).
Fourth: as for the subject of the prophecy, it is: "Thus speaketh the LORD of hosts, saying, This people say, The time is not come, the time that the LORD's house should be built" [2].

He begins his speech with the people by saying, "the LORD of hosts speaketh," as though he wanted to assure them that if they work for the sake of His Kingdom they are His soldiers and He is their commander, who knows nothing but spiritual striving without slackness; He is the Lord of hosts! Perhaps he also meant to rebuke them: if they had left the work in slackness and carelessness, He is not in need of working hands, for He is the Lord of the heavenly hosts... yet He calls them to work because He loves them and longs to work through them.

At the beginning of His speech He does not say "My people" but "this people." In our study of the book of Exodus and some of the books of the prophets we noticed that when the people sin He does not call them "His people," that is, He does not ascribe them to Himself, as happened in His speaking with Moses, when He said to him: "Thy people have corrupted themselves" (Ex 32:7), ascribing the people to Moses and not to Himself. But when the people are sanctified, it is sweet to Him to boast of them, counting them His people, their Sabbaths His Sabbaths, their feasts His feasts, and their offerings His offerings.

The secret of God's grief over this people is that they set up arguments and justifications for refraining from the work, saying: The time is not come to build the house of the Lord. They pretended that the external opposition was a divine sign that the time for the work had not yet come, and perhaps they also justified it by saying that they should first take care of their own houses so that their families might be at rest, and then they would work for the house of the Lord with a restful heart, and they did not realize that God should be first in their lives, as the Lord says: "But seek ye first the kingdom of God, and his righteousness; and all these things shall be added unto you" (Mt 6:33).

Our life is in reality a series of opportunities; if an opportunity is lost it may not be repeated. It is not fitting for us to say, "The time is not yet come," lest we become like Felix the governor, who postponed the opportunity of repentance until he should find a convenient season (Acts 24:25), and we never heard that he found the time. Rather it befits us to say: "But exhort one another daily, while it is called To day; lest any of you be hardened through the deceitfulness of sin" (v. 3:13), "Redeeming the time, because the days are evil" (Eph 5:16).

entries.section: 2. A rebuke for caring about temporal things:

paragraphs.text: 3 Then came the word of the LORD by Haggai the prophet, saying, 4 "Is it time for you, O ye, to dwell in your cieled houses, and this house lie waste? 5 Now therefore thus saith the LORD of hosts; Consider your ways. 6 Ye have sown much, and bring in little; ye eat, but ye have not enough; ye drink, but ye are not filled with drink; ye clothe you, but there is none warm; and he that earneth wages earneth wages to put it into a bag with holes. 7 Thus saith the LORD of hosts; Consider your ways. 8 Go up to the mountain, and bring wood, and build the house; and I will take pleasure in it, and I will be glorified, saith the LORD. 9 Ye looked for much, and, lo, it came to little; and when ye brought it home, I did blow upon it. Why? saith the LORD of hosts. Because of mine house that is waste, and ye run every man unto his own house. 10 Therefore the heaven over you is stayed from dew, and the earth is stayed from her fruit. 11 And I called for a drought upon the land, and upon the mountains, and upon the corn, and upon the new wine, and upon the oil, and upon that which the ground bringeth forth, and upon men, and upon cattle, and upon all the labour of the hands."

At the very time when they say that the time has not come to build the house of the Lord, they themselves dwell in cieled houses of their own, fit for kings (1 Kgs 7:7; Jer 22:14), as though they not only put temporal things before eternal things, but even in their management of temporal matters they dwelt in luxurious palaces fit for kings and great men.

entries.section: 2. A rebuke for caring about temporal things:

paragraphs.text: Even if they dwell in sumptuous palaces, it behooves them to return to themselves and reflect on their lives anew, for He says to them: "Consider your ways" [5]. Perhaps the word "heart" here means reflection on the inner life or self-examination, as the Apostle says: "Let every man prove his own work" (Gal 6:4), that is, judge himself before others judge him... And here the prophet helps them to examine themselves, saying: "Ye have sown much, and bring in little; ye eat, but ye have not enough; ye drink, but ye are not filled with drink; ye clothe you, but there is none warm; and he that earneth wages earneth wages to put it into a bag with holes" [6].

When man refuses to cling to God his Creator, he refuses blessing in his life; nature resists him and the earth does not give him its fruit; even his body does not enjoy satiety and sufficiency, however much is offered to it. He may sow much, but the harvest is little; he may eat greedily all that he desires, but without being satisfied; and he receives wages without measure, but he is like one who puts them in a bag with holes. This is what Scripture warns of in more than one place. Scripture says: "And when I have broken the staff of your bread, ten women shall bake your bread in one oven, and they shall deliver you your bread again by weight: and ye shall eat, and not be satisfied" (Lev 26:26); "Thou shalt eat, and not be satisfied; and thy hunger shall be in thy belly... thou shalt sow, but thou shalt not reap; thou shalt tread the olives, but thou shalt not anoint thee with oil; and sweet wine, but shalt not drink wine" (Mic 6:14-15; see Hos 4:10).

St. Clement of Alexandria sees that the owner of the bag with holes is the one who gathers his money and shuts it up, so that he gives nothing to others, for he says: [He who gathers his wheat and shuts it up, who gives to no one, falls into a poorer state]. For this reason, when St. Jerome praised the blind priest Epiphanius, he said to him: [You do not put your wages in a bag with holes, but you lay up your treasures in heaven]. And in the Conferences of St. John Cassian, Abba Abraham says: [The owner of the bag with holes is the one who hears the words of others but loses them because of his lack of self-control and the lack of concentration of his mind].

entries.section: 2. A rebuke for caring about temporal things:

paragraphs.text: Thus man loses blessing even in temporal matters by withdrawing from the Source of blessing. This the Lord affirms once more, threatening not for vengeance but to bring man back to Himself, saying: "Because of mine house that is waste, and ye run every man unto his own house, therefore the heaven over you is stayed from dew, and the earth is stayed from her fruit. And I called for a drought upon the land, and upon the mountains, and upon the corn, and upon the new wine, and upon the oil, and upon that which the ground bringeth forth, and upon men, and upon all the labour of the hands" [11].

When man ignores his Creator, creation ignores him: the heavens withhold their dew and the earth its produce, and even the air loses its gentleness, so that man, animals and plants are suffocated by its heat, on the mountains and in the level regions, spoiling all the labor of the hands. It is written in the book of Deuteronomy: "And thy heaven that is over thy head shall be brass, and the earth that is under thee shall be iron. The LORD shall make the rain of thy land powder and dust: from heaven shall it come down upon thee, until thou be destroyed" (Deut 28:23-24). When man hardens his heart, heaven becomes for him hard as brass and the earth iron without fruit, and as his thoughts are earthly and dusty, the rain turns for him into dust that destroys him... as though nature offers him what is hidden within him.

In the Septuagint it reads: "And I called for the sword upon the earth and upon the mountains... etc." The wrath of nature against him is not enough; rather, he loses his peace with his brothers, who pursue him with the sword wherever he is found, even if he hides in the mountains among the rocks, and they scatter by violence all his fruits.

We can also interpret the divine words "Because of mine house that is waste, and ye run every man unto his own house" in this way: He means His inner dwelling in us, which becomes waste through its loss of God Himself as its dweller, so the soul runs to its own house, that is, it curls up around itself and clings to its selfishness; then, instead of gain, it enters into loss and complete deprivation, for the soul (the heavens) loses the grace of God (the dew) and is deprived of the work of the Holy Spirit, and the earth withholds its produce, that is, the body loses its holiness, so there is in it no fruit that gladdens God and man, and its life turns into great turmoil, where the inner sword pursues it wherever it is found. The sword shatters its earth, that is, its body, and its mountains, that is, its lofty abilities, and spoils its corn and its new wine and its oil, that is, spoils its food and its drink and its medicine, to leave it hungry, thirsty and sick!

God does not leave us thus, but offers the remedy: "Thus saith the LORD of hosts; Consider your ways. Go up to the mountain, and bring wood, and build the house; and I will take pleasure in it, and I will be glorified" [7-8].

a. The remedy begins with the saying: "Consider your ways." There is no reform of the soul without man's examining himself, not only by calling himself to account for his outward or visible conduct, but by reflection on the heart itself. For if this book is the book of building the inner house of the Lord, it lifts our thought to the inside of the heart as the center of the work. It is as though He says: Prepare your heart so that the Lord may establish His dwelling in you by His Holy Spirit.

b. The matter does not stop at mere reflection on the heart, but He says: "Go up to the mountain"... Instead of our lofty mountain, that is, the (ego) that brings us down into the abyss, we ascend to the mountain of which the prophet Daniel spoke: "The stone that smote the image became a great mountain, and filled the whole earth" (Dan 2:35). This is the mountain of which it was said: "A city that is set on an hill cannot be hid" (Mt 5:14).

Let us then ascend with the Lord Himself, to be founded upon Him as a mountain that fills the earth and lifts us up as a shining city and a holy temple, for He is the Rock of our faith. There we bring wood to build the house of the Lord, that is, we carry His Cross and share with Him in His sufferings, for the sanctuaries of the Lord are not established in us apart from His sufferings.

c. Finally He says: "Build the house; and I will take pleasure in it, and I will be glorified." Although He is the Builder of the house, as the Psalmist says: "Except the LORD build the house, they labour in vain that build it," yet He affirms, "Build the house," confirming His sanctification of human freedom; He does not establish the house in us without our will or without us, but ascribes the work to us although He is the One working in us.

12 Then Zerubbabel the son of Shealtiel, and Joshua the son of Josedech, the high priest, with all the remnant of the people, heard the voice of the LORD their God, and the words of Haggai the prophet, as the LORD their God had sent him, and the people did fear before the LORD. 13 Then spake Haggai the LORD's messenger in the LORD's message unto the people, saying, "I am with you, saith the LORD." 14 And the LORD stirred up the spirit of Zerubbabel the son of Shealtiel, governor of Judah, and the spirit of Joshua the son of Josedech, the high priest, and the spirit of all the remnant of the people; and they came and did work in the house of the LORD of hosts, their God, 15 in the four and twentieth day of the sixth month, in the second year of Darius the king.

The prophetic words came with their joyful fruit, for the governor, the priest and all the remnant of the people heard the words of the Lord and feared before His face and began to work. It is as though, when man listens to the divine words, his will (the governor) submits, his heart (the priest) bows, and all his energies (the remnant of the people) respond, so that he is filled in his entirety with the fear of the Lord and works with power through a joyful inner harmony.

entries.section: 1. The temple, the desire of all nations:

paragraphs.text: 1 In the seventh month, in the one and twentieth day of the month, came the word of the LORD by the prophet Haggai, saying, 2 "Speak now to Zerubbabel the son of Shealtiel, governor of Judah, and to Joshua the son of Josedech, the high priest, and to the residue of the people, saying, 3 Who is left among you that saw this house in her first glory? and how do ye see it now? is it not in your eyes in comparison of it as nothing? 4 Yet now be strong, O Zerubbabel, saith the LORD; and be strong, O Joshua, son of Josedech, the high priest; and be strong, all ye people of the land, saith the LORD, and work: for I am with you, saith the LORD of hosts: 5 According to the word that I covenanted with you when ye came out of Egypt, so my spirit remaineth among you: fear ye not. 6 For thus saith the LORD of hosts; Yet once, it is a little while, and I will shake the heavens, and the earth, and the sea, and the dry land; 7 And I will shake all nations, and the desire of all nations shall come: and I will fill this house with glory, saith the LORD of hosts. 8 The silver is mine, and the gold is mine, saith the LORD of hosts. 9 The glory of this latter house shall be greater than of the former, saith the LORD of hosts: and in this place will I give peace, saith the LORD of hosts."

The second message came when the builders had begun the work about a month earlier, so it was a message of encouragement and support for them. If the previous prophecy had wounded them with rebuke, this prophecy bandages their wounds with encouraging words of divine comfort.

The date of this prophecy is "the seventh month, in the one and twentieth day of the month," that is, the seventh day of the Feast of Tabernacles, the last harvest feast of the Jewish year (see Lev 23:39-44). This feast was marked by joy and by thanksgiving sacrifices, offered on the last days of the feast more than on any other day.

It was fitting for all to be filled with joy, not only because of the feast but because of the beginning of the work on the house of the Lord, and to offer thanksgiving sacrifices to God, who was restoring to them the glory that had been taken from them. But the enemy of good cannot bear the joy and thanksgiving of the children of God, so he tried to crush them by sowing thoughts of despair through some of the elderly who had lived in the days of the old temple before it was destroyed (about seventy years earlier). These compared the old temple with the foundations of the new one and counted the work in progress as nothing before the splendor of the glory of the old. While the priests and Levites were singing with joy and sounding the trumpets for the work, these elderly men began to weep bitterly over the glory of the old temple. The situation almost became critical, and the enemy of good nearly turned the joyful work into sorrow, heaviness of heart and the crushing of souls.

entries.section: 1. The temple, the desire of all nations:

paragraphs.text: Thus some of the elderly err by despising the work of the new generation, counting their works, when compared with former works, as nothing [3]. Therefore the wise man counsels us: "Say not thou, What is the cause that the former days were better than these?" (Eccl 7:10).
And in order to remove the spirit of despair, God began to support and encourage them in this way.

entries.section: 1. The temple, the desire of all nations:

paragraphs.text: First: "Be strong, O Zerubbabel; be strong, O Joshua; and be strong, all ye people of the land, and work: for I am with you" [4]. It is as though He asks the governor, the priest and the people not to be occupied with comparisons between old and new, but to work with strength, being strong for the sake of "God" who dwells in their midst. May every believer not squander his energy on the many thoughts that crush people, but let his will be strengthened, let his heart be strengthened, and let all his powers be strengthened, working with all his power, sure that the Lord is with him, which is the secret of his joy and his glory!

entries.section: 1. The temple, the desire of all nations:

paragraphs.text: If the purpose of the building is that the Lord may meet with them through the covenant and that they may enjoy His dwelling in their midst, then in the midst of the work He says to them: "According to the word that I covenanted with you when ye came out of Egypt, so my spirit remaineth among you: fear ye not" [5]. It is as though He says: Do not fear, for I enter into the covenant with you, and My Spirit dwells in your midst as long as you are working... and this is the true glory.

entries.section: 1. The temple, the desire of all nations:

paragraphs.text: Second: "Yet once, it is a little while, and I will shake the heavens, and the earth, and the sea, and the dry land; and I will shake all nations, and the desire of all nations shall come: and I will fill this house with glory, saith the LORD of hosts" [6-7]. In the past, when He established the covenant at Mount Sinai, the Lord shook the place and the mountain smoked. Now He shakes heaven (the soul), earth (the body), the sea (the gifts) and the dry land (the energies). He breaks down the old man in order to raise up in us the new man, so that we bear his marks in our souls, and our bodies, our gifts and our energies are sanctified. With the shaking of the old nature we receive a new life, raised up and in harmony in body and soul, and we work for the sake of the Kingdom.

This shaking is the sign of the coming of "the desire of all nations," for He dwells within us in the waters of Baptism, when we are buried with Him, so that the powers of darkness are shaken and our outward man is broken down. And when He comes also at the end of the ages, nature will be shaken with power, so that the material world passes away and the Lord comes as a heavenly and eternal King.

Some translate "the desire of all nations shall come" as "the wealth of all nations shall come," meaning that the new temple is filled with splendor by the entrance of the Gentiles into the membership of the Church, offering their faith in the Savior and their zeal as the secret of spiritual wealth.

entries.section: 1. The temple, the desire of all nations:

paragraphs.text: Third: "The silver is mine, and the gold is mine, saith the LORD of hosts" [8]. If the measures of glory were the abundance of gold, silver and precious stones that filled the old temple, then in the new house the Lord says: "Provide neither gold, nor silver, nor brass in your purses" (Mt 10:9), since He Himself is our silver and our gold, He is the adornment of the house and its glory.

St. John Chrysostom sees that the prophet spoke this phrase because many of the Jews found it hard to believe how the old temple could return again with its gold and silver after it had become dust and ashes. It is as though the Lord says to them: [Why do they not believe, for the silver is Mine and the gold is Mine; I do not need to borrow from anyone to adorn My house?].

entries.section: 1. The temple, the desire of all nations:

paragraphs.text: Fourth: "The glory of this latter house shall be greater than of the former, saith the LORD of hosts: and in this place will I give peace, saith the LORD of hosts" [9]. If we compare the glory of the first temple, which Solomon built, with that of the latter, which Zerubbabel built, we find that the first was greater in the precious stones and gold it contained and in the magnificence of the building. It is also recorded in the Babylonian Talmud that the temple of Zerubbabel lacked five things that the temple of Solomon had: the glory of the Shekinah, the holy fire, the Ark of the Covenant, the Urim and Thummim, and the spirit of prophecy. But here He lifts us up not to the temple of Zerubbabel but to the temple to which the Lord referred as being His body (Jn 2). How glorious is the new temple in which reconciliation between the Father and mankind was accomplished through the shedding of blood (Col 1:20)! Therefore He says: "And in this place will I give peace, saith the LORD of hosts."

entries.section: 1. The temple, the desire of all nations:

paragraphs.text: If God disciplined His people by captivity, so that the temple of Solomon was destroyed, it was only to bring them back to build the temple in a greater glory; thus the Lord disciplines us to grant us a better splendor, as St. John Chrysostom said [11].

entries.section: 2. God seeks the temple of the heart:

paragraphs.text: 10 In the four and twentieth day of the ninth month, in the second year of Darius, came the word of the LORD by Haggai the prophet, saying, 11 "Thus saith the LORD of hosts; Ask now the priests concerning the law, saying, 12 If one bear holy flesh in the skirt of his garment, and with his skirt do touch bread, or pottage, or wine, or oil, or any meat, shall it be holy?" And the priests answered and said, "No." 13 Then said Haggai, "If one that is unclean by a dead body touch any of these, shall it be unclean?" And the priests answered and said, "It shall be unclean." 14 Then answered Haggai, and said, "So is this people, and so is this nation before me, saith the LORD; and so is every work of their hands; and that which they offer there is unclean. 15 And now, I pray you, consider from this day and upward, from before a stone was laid upon a stone in the temple of the LORD: 16 Since those days were, when one came to an heap of twenty measures, there were but ten: when one came to the pressfat for to draw out fifty vessels out of the press, there were but twenty. 17 I smote you with blasting and with mildew and with hail in all the labours of your hands; yet ye turned not to me, saith the LORD. 18 Consider now from this day and upward, from the four and twentieth day of the ninth month, even from the day that the foundation of the LORD'S temple was laid, consider it. 19 Is the seed yet in the barn? yea, as yet the vine, and the fig tree, and the pomegranate, and the olive tree, hath not brought forth: from this day will I bless you."

This prophecy came after the previous one, two months after it was declared. In it he makes clear that if the glory of the temple is the Lord's dwelling in the midst of His people, then the purpose of the temple is the sanctification of the heart. Therefore He asks us not to fix our minds on the building of stone but on the heart. For if we raise the building of stone with defiled hearts, what benefit is it? The following is to be noted in this prophecy:

First: God asks the prophet to ask the priests about the law, although he is a prophet. God had sent the prophet to urge the priests to work, yet He asks him to ask the priests for the interpretation of the law. It is as though every member of the Church works with the other in his own work, with no preference of one over the other except in respect of faithfulness in what has been entrusted to him: the prophet in prophecy and the priest in interpreting the law.

If the principal work of the priest is to interpret the law, as St. Jerome says: [Great is the work of the priesthood, to answer questions concerning the law... For in fact, deficiency in the priest's teaching hinders him from doing good to others... and as much as he builds up the Church of Christ by the virtues of his life, he harms it all the more by his failure to resist those who drag it downward.]

Second: If a man bears holy flesh in the skirt of his garment and with his skirt touches something, it does not make it holy; but if he has been defiled by a dead body, what he touches he defiles. It is as though He wanted to affirm that contagion passes to the lives of others more quickly in sin than in holiness, because demolishing is quicker than building. It is as though He asks them to care for their spiritual health and sanctification, because every sickness and uncleanness is transmitted and spreads among them quickly.

entries.section: 2. God seeks the temple of the heart:

paragraphs.text: Third: He says, "If one bear holy flesh," and He did not say "a holy sacrifice." When they insist on evil, God does not accept from them the building of His house, however magnificent and beautiful it may seem, and does not accept their sacrifices but sees them as "flesh." He asks them to examine themselves, lest while they are occupied with the outward building they lose the sanctification of the heart, for He says: "And now, I pray you, consider from this day and upward, from before a stone was laid upon a stone in the temple of the LORD" [15].

entries.section: 2. God seeks the temple of the heart:

paragraphs.text: Fourth: Since the heart is not sanctified, even if they build a temple for the Lord in their midst they do not enjoy the blessing, for He says: "Since those days were, when one came to an heap of twenty measures, there were but ten: when one came to the pressfat for to draw out fifty vessels out of the press, there were but twenty. I smote you with blasting and with mildew and with hail in all the labours of your hands; yet ye turned not to me, saith the LORD" [16-17]. A man comes to the threshing floor expecting to gather twenty measures of grain, and he gathers only ten; he comes to the winepress to draw out fifty vessels of the juice of the grapes and finds only twenty. As for the plants, He strikes them with blasting (the blowing of a violent wind), with mildew (pests) and with hail. Thus nature opposes him, perhaps to bring him back to his Creator.

entries.section: 3. The new temple and the divine seal:

paragraphs.text: 20 And again the word of the LORD came unto Haggai in the four and twentieth day of the month, saying, 21 "Speak to Zerubbabel, governor of Judah, saying, I will shake the heavens and the earth; 22 And I will overthrow the throne of kingdoms, and I will destroy the strength of the kingdoms of the heathen; and I will overthrow the chariots, and those that ride in them; and the horses and their riders shall come down, every one by the sword of his brother. 23 In that day, saith the LORD of hosts, will I take thee, O Zerubbabel, my servant, the son of Shealtiel, saith the LORD, and will make thee as a signet: for I have chosen thee, saith the LORD of hosts."

This last prophecy was declared on the very day on which the previous prophecy was declared. In the former the Lord affirms the necessity of directing eyes to the temple of the heart and its sanctification, so that the believer may be filled with blessing and enjoy the Lord's dwelling within him; but here the speech is directed to Zerubbabel the governor, who was of the seed of David, declaring that He blesses him by breaking down the opposing pagan nations and by setting him as a signet for the Lord, as the one chosen from His heart.

If Zerubbabel represents the Lord Christ, who was "born in Babylon," in that He took our body and came to our earth and entered with us even into the tomb, yet He is the only Son, in whom the Father is well pleased, and in Him we have become God's chosen ones (Eph 1:4). In Him we enjoy victory, not over human nations with their chariots and horses, but over the evil powers of darkness.

By Baptism the works of the old man are defeated under our feet like collapsing pagan nations, and we enjoy the heavenly seal, which the bride longed for, saying: "Set me as a seal upon thine heart, as a seal upon thine arm" (Song 8:6). By it we have become like a signet, bearing the honor of the Lord, His riches and His spiritual authority, and we bear witness to Him as a bride united with Him on a transcendent level.
